prompt: In a study, $300$ volunteers were randomly assigned to either a new exercise program or no program. Those in the program showed significantly lower resting heart rates. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.label: The exercise program likely caused the lower heart rates among these volunteers
The exercise program lowers heart rates for all adults
Lower heart rates cause people to exercise more
No conclusion about cause can be drawn from this study

hint: The volunteers were *randomly assigned* to the groups. What does that permit?

hints.text: The volunteers were *randomly assigned* to the groups. What does that permit?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try the contrast: a survey asking who already exercises can only show an association, but randomly assigning people to exercise or not can show cause. The design decides what you may claim.
Random assignment to treatments allows a causal conclusion.
But the volunteers were not randomly selected from all adults, so the conclusion stays with them.

learningObjective: Distinguish what random assignment and random selection each justify.
explanation: Random *assignment* to treatment groups controls for confounding variables, so a causal claim is justified — that is what makes this an experiment rather than an observational study.
But the participants were volunteers, not a random sample of all adults, so the result cannot be generalized beyond them. That rules out choice B.
Choice C reverses the direction the design established, and choice D wrongly denies that random assignment supports causation.

alternativeExplanations.title: The two-by-two that answers every one of these
steps: Random selection + random assignment: cause, generalizable to the whole population.
Random assignment only (volunteers): cause, but only for the participants — this study.
Random selection only (survey): generalizable, but association only, never cause. Neither: association among participants only.
